Expectation1: Communicate any challenges or concerns promptly to the mentor.
Situation1: The mentee has a small question about terminology that isn't blocking their work.
Expectation2: Challenge unfair systems and influence policy change
Situation2: They gather recurring cases of unfair treatment and bring them to discussions with community leaders or officials.
Story:
I sat at my desk, staring at the email draft to my mentor. As a mentee, I was supposed to communicate any challenges or concerns promptly, but my question about terminology felt so minor—barely a blip in my workflow. I hesitated, not wanting to waste my mentor’s time with something I could probably figure out on my own. Yet, I knew the expectation: transparency, no matter how small the issue.

At the same time, my phone buzzed with another message from a community member. As an advocate, I was collecting stories of unfair treatment, building a case to present to the local officials. Every detail mattered, every voice counted. I was expected to challenge the system, to be thorough and relentless in surfacing even the smallest injustices.

The contradiction gnawed at me. In one role, I was supposed to filter out the trivial; in the other, I was supposed to amplify every concern, no matter how small. My mind spun with the weight of these expectations, torn between not wanting to bother my mentor and knowing that, as an advocate, I would urge anyone else to speak up. My fingers hovered over the keyboard, caught in the tension of what to do next.
